Good morning...
I’m Ashutosh Joshi in Mumbai, where traders have plenty to chew on as they return from a holiday.
Jensen Huang is back! India’s midweek break meant we missed bringing you the Nvidia CEO’s dramatic comeback. The news saw the AI trade storm back, though the enthusiasm lasted just one session, with tech stocks turning lower again. That suggests India’s status as an anti-AI haven may still be intact.
It isn’t just Huang who is back — the threat of Donald Trump’s tariffs has resurfaced too. The US is set to soon announce plans to raise levies on goods from more than a dozen economies, according to people familiar with the matter. India and the US could conclude negotiations on a trade deal soon, though signing and implementing it may take longer, a top government official said last week.
The latest developments will test the bullish mood among India investors, particularly as the recent surge has left local stocks looking pricey compared with global peers, as we write in the Markets Buzz section. The benchmark NSE Nifty 50 slid 1.8% on Monday after a four-week winning streak fueled by this month’s record foreign inflows.
Shares of Tata Steel and APL Apollo Tubes will be in focus again today after the two stocks erased a combined about $3.2 billion in market value on Monday. Asian stocks retreated after a selloff in US technology shares revived doubts about the durability of the artificial intelligence trade, extending losses from Wall Street into the region. Gold fell.
The MSCI Asia Pacific Index slipped 2%, giving up some gains from Tuesday’s rally that was the biggest since July. The Kospi Index in South Korea lost 4.5% and the Taiwanese benchmark 5% as the two key barometers of the AI trade in Asia came under pressure. Futures for the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 indexes both fell at least 0.4%.

Australia’s core inflation unexpectedly accelerated in October, highlighting persistent price pressures in the economy and vindicating Reserve Bank officials’ hawkish commentary.
Money markets pushed back bets on the timing of a 2027 interest-rate cut after the annual trimmed mean gauge of consumer prices advanced 3.8%, exceeding a 3.6% forecast, government data showed Wednesday. Core prices rose 0.5% from the prior month, also overshooting estimates, as did headline inflation.

Australia signed a new treaty with the Solomon Islands aimed at rolling back China’s access to the Pacific, partly reversing Beijing’s gains in the region three years ago that alarmed the US and its allies.
The agreement, signed Wednesday in Canberra, is the culmination of Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s efforts to counter a 2022 deal that offered China security access to the Pacific island nation, signed just before he took office.

Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
India’s biggest pension funds are directing more of their inflows to government bonds as they near a regulatory threshold on equity investments, just as local stocks rebound from a bruising selloff.
UTI Pension Fund is directing half of its incremental investments into government bonds, compared with none last year. SBI Pension Funds says stocks will account for only a quarter of its new investments, down from about 60% in the three months through June. The two money managers account for 58% of the nation’s $193 billion in retirement assets.

Ho Chi Minh City Development JSC Bank is planning to both sell global bonds and borrow via the syndicated loan market, turning to overseas investors to meet rising credit demand in an economy chasing ambitious growth goals.
HDBank, as the lender is known, plans to issue up to $500 million of global bonds by early next year, becoming the first Vietnamese bank to list debt securities in the UK, HDBank Chairman Kim Byoungho said in an interview from Ho Chi Minh City. The bonds will likely have a three-year maturity.

Australia’s financial conditions are “clearly restrictive” following five interest-rate increases this year, a senior Reserve Bank official said, while also noting the difficulty of determining the extent.
“Policy is clearly having a material effect in interest-sensitive areas, particularly housing,” the RBA’s Head of Domestic Markets David Jacobs said in a speech at a Sydney conference on Wednesday. “But credit spreads remain low and business borrowing has been remarkably strong.”

item.title: Icahn’s Fortune Sinks to $1.3b as Debt Pressures Rise
item.description: Carl Icahn’s fortune has dwindled to about $1.3 billion as mounting debt squeezes his business empire, leaving the longtime corporate raider and activist investor facing one of the toughest stretches of his career. When Icahn Enterprises reported third-quarter earnings this month, it warned there was no assurance it could refinance $1.4 billion of bonds due in May on acceptable terms — or at all. Since then, the pressure has only intensified. Shares of CVR Energy, a key IEP holding, have tumbled about 40% since it agreed earlier this month to buy two additional refineries, eroding the value of a stake that accounted for about half of Icahn’s publicly traded investment partnership at the end of September. Yields on some of IEP’s 2029 bonds now exceed 30%, and the company has about $4.4 billion of bonds outstanding. Tom Maloney, Bloomberg News Editor, discusses how lots of leverage of led to Carl Icahn's investment losses. (Source: Bloomberg)
